text: The emerald ash borer (Agrilus planipennis), a green buprestid beetle native to temperate northeastern Asia—including Russia, Mongolia, northern China, Japan, and Korea—is native to that region where it typically occurs at low densities and does not cause significant damage to ash trees (Fraxinus spp.). Females lay eggs in bark crevices, flakes, or cracks, and the eggs, measuring 0.6 to 1.0 mm in diameter and initially white, turn reddish-brown if fertile, hatch about two weeks later, and the larvae chew through the bark to feed on the phloem, cambium, and outer xylem, creating long serpentine galleries. The larvae go through four instars, with fully mature fourth-instar larvae being 26 to 32 mm long; they excavate J-shaped chambers in the sapwood or outer bark in the fall, where they develop into pupae and emerge as adults the following spring. Adults are bright metallic green, about 8.5 mm long and 1.6 mm wide, with darker green elytra that may have copper hues, and a small spine at the tip of the abdomen; they have serrate antennae beginning at the fourth segment. Adults emerge after 400–500 degree-days above 10 °C (50 °F), peaking at around 1,000 degree-days, feed on ash leaves for one week before mating, and males locate females by visual cues, dropping directly onto them to mate, with mating lasting up to 50 minutes and females mating with multiple males. A typical female lives about six weeks and lays 40–70 eggs, with longer-lived females laying up to 200. Larvae can overwinter in their galleries and may require an additional summer of feeding before overwintering again, with a two-year life cycle more common in cool climates like European Russia. The beetle is invasive in North America, where it was first identified in Canton, Michigan in 2002 (though possibly present since the late 1980s), likely introduced via shipping materials such as packing crates, and has a core population in Michigan and surrounding states and provinces, spreading to Ontario, northern Louisiana, Nebraska, New Brunswick, Colorado, and the Pacific Northwest (Oregon), with a population found in Moscow, Russia in 2003, spreading westward at up to 40 km (25 mi) per year and expected to reach central Europe between 2031 and 2036. It has spread to far eastern Ukraine from Russia and is not recorded in the European Union as of 2019. In North America, it primarily infests green ash (F. pennsylvanica), black ash (F. nigra), white ash (F. americana), and blue ash (F. quadrangulata), with blue ash showing higher resistance due to high tannin content in its leaves, a trait absent in most American ash species except blue ash. In Europe, F. excelsior is the main host, moderately resistant to infestation. The beetle can also infest non-ash species such as white fringe tree and Olea europaea (in lab settings), though it is unclear if these trees were healthy when infested. Ash trees in pure stands or in landscaping are more vulnerable due to environmental stresses like compacted soil, pollution, road salt, and urban heat, and because most landscaping ashes come from a few cultivars with low genetic diversity. Damage occurs as larval feeding disrupts nutrient and water transport, effectively girdling the tree and killing it; stressed trees may regenerate via stump sprouting or produce higher seed crops. Without natural suppressors like resistant trees, predators, or parasitoid wasps present in its native range, populations grow rapidly and all ash trees in an area are expected to die within 10 years. Every North American ash species is susceptible, though some Asian ash species like F. baroniana, F. chinensis, F. floribunda, F. mandshurica, and F. platypoda are resistant. In North America, the beetle has killed tens of millions of ash trees and threatens to kill most of the 8.7 billion ash trees, eliminating nearly all ash trees in the National Capital Region in nine years, reducing the density from 17–18 per hectare to 5–6 per hectare and transforming ash-dominated swamplands into shrublands, impacting wildlife. The loss of ash affects soil nutrients, increases invasive plants, and alters species that depend on ash. Control efforts include monitoring via visual surveys and traps using purple or green colors or volatile pheromones, girdling trees as trap trees, and quarantines restricting transport of ash firewood or live plants without inspection or treatment. Infested trees are often removed in urban areas, with replacements using non-ash species like maple, oak, or linden, and in rural areas, trees may be harvested for lumber or firewood under quarantine. Insecticides such as azadirachtin, imidacloprid, emamectin benzoate, and dinotefuran are used, with dinotefuran and imidacloprid being systemic and effective for one to three years; treatments are typically applied via direct injection or soil drench and are mainly used in urban areas with high-value trees, though not feasible for large forested areas. Insecticide use does not stop damage progression. The U.S. Department of Agriculture's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service ended all EAB quarantine activities on 14 December 2020 due to ineffectiveness, shifting focus to biological controls. Government agencies in the U.S. and Canada use the native parasitoid wasp Cerceris fumipennis for biological surveillance—volunteers catch the wasps as they return with beetles, indicating infestation—without significantly reducing beetle populations. The native range of the emerald ash borer in Asia was surveyed for parasitoid species that target the beetle without attacking other insects, in hopes they could suppress populations when introduced.

It is recommended to choose monotypic species such as the pawpaw, yellowwood, Franklin tree, Kentucky coffeetree, Osage orange, sourwood, and bald cypress. Insecticides containing active ingredients like azadirachtin, imidacloprid, emamectin benzoate, and dinotefuran are currently used; dinotefuran and imidacloprid are systemic and remain effective for one to three years depending on the product.[8][47][48] Insecticides are generally only considered viable in urban areas with high-value trees near an infestation.[47] Ash trees are primarily treated through direct injection into the tree or soil drench, and some insecticides require licensed applicators due to application restrictions. Damage from emerald ash borer can continue to increase over time even with insecticide use.[8] Insecticide treatments are not practical for large forested areas outside of urban settings.[8] The native range of emerald ash borer in Asia was surveyed for parasitoid species that target emerald ash borer without attacking other insects, with the goal of introducing them to suppress populations in North America.[49] Three species imported from China were approved for release: Spathius agrili, Tetrastichus planipennisi, and Oobius agrili by the USDA in 2007 and in Canada in 2013, and Spathius galinae was approved for release in 2015.[50][51] Excluding Spathius galinae, which was recently released, the other three species have been documented parasitizing emerald ash borer larvae one year after release, showing survival through winter, though establishment varied by species and location.[51] Tetrastichus planipennisi and Oobius agrili have established and shown increasing populations in Michigan since 2008; Spathius agrili has had lower establishment success in North America, possibly due to a lack of available emerald ash borer larvae at adult emergence in spring, limited cold tolerance, and better suitability to regions below the 40th parallel.[51] The USDA is also evaluating the use of Beauveria bassiana, an insect fungal pathogen, in combination with parasitoid wasps for controlling emerald ash borer.[52]
